steps.tx: Suspect **monogenic diabetes** when diabetes presents before 6 months of age, when a young lean adult has a strong autosomal dominant family history and negative **islet antibodies**, or when diabetes travels with renal cysts, deafness, or a syndromic picture. Do not label every antibody-negative young adult as type 2 diabetes. The antibody result and the family pattern are what open this diagnosis.

left.title: Think monogenic
points: Lean young adult, autosomal dominant family, negative islet antibodies
Diabetes with renal cysts, deafness, or a syndrome

right.title: Do not assume type 2
points: Antibody-negative is not the same as type 2
A syndromic partner changes the gene
Treatment can be a sulfonylurea or no drug at all

steps.tx: **GCK-MODY** causes stable mild **fasting hyperglycemia**, often 100 to 144 mg/dL, that does not progress like type 2 diabetes and usually needs no treatment outside pregnancy. HbA1c remains near the top of the nondiabetic range for life. The glucokinase sensor is set high, so insulin is released at a higher glucose. Pregnancy is the situation that can change the no-treatment plan.

vis.alt: Beta cell with a glucose transporter, glucokinase as the glucose sensor, a nuclear transcription factor, and insulin granules.
vis.caption: A beta cell with its glucose transporter, glucokinase as the sensor, a nuclear transcription factor, and insulin secretory granules. GCK-MODY is the sensor set high. HNF1A-MODY is the transcription-factor side of the same drawing. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: **HNF1A-MODY** is sensitive to a low-dose **sulfonylurea**, which is first-line drug therapy, and the diabetes progresses, unlike GCK-MODY. HNF4A-MODY is similar and also causes fetal macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia. **HNF1B** disease is diabetes plus renal cysts, genital malformations, and **hypomagnesemia**. The renal cysts are the clue that this is not HNF1A-MODY.

steps.tx: **Neonatal diabetes** that is diagnosed before 6 months is often a **KCNJ11** or **ABCC8** variant in the KATP channel. Many of these infants can be transferred from insulin to a **sulfonylurea**. Diabetes that starts after 6 to 12 months is much more often type 1. A sulfonylurea is considered after the channel gene is known, not for every infant on insulin.

left.title: Before 6 months
points: Many infants move from insulin to a sulfonylurea
This is neonatal diabetes, not routine type 1

right.title: After 6 to 12 months
points: Do not promise a sulfonylurea switch

steps.tx: **Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness** is the mitochondrial variant m.3243A-G. **Metformin** is used cautiously because of the lactic acidosis risk in mitochondrial disease. Inheritance is maternal, so an affected father does not transmit it. Deafness plus diabetes on the mother's side is the pattern that should trigger this test.

steps.tx: **Wolfram syndrome**, also called **DIDMOAD**, is diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, **optic atrophy**, and deafness, from WFS1. Optic atrophy in a child with diabetes is not ordinary retinopathy. The optic disc is pale, which is a different finding from background retinal spots. Diabetes insipidus in the same child is part of the syndrome.

left.title: Wolfram syndrome
points: Diabetes insipidus can be part of it

right.title: Ordinary diabetic retinopathy
points: Does not pale the disc as the first finding

steps.tx: Generalized **lipodystrophy** causes severe insulin resistance, low **leptin**, and hypertriglyceridemia. **Metreleptin** is replacement for generalized lipodystrophy. Finding almost no subcutaneous fat changes the treatment away from ordinary type 2 drugs. The drawing is acquired generalised lipodystrophy, and it does not show an injection of metreleptin.

vis.caption: Acquired generalised lipodystrophy, spelled that way on the figure: subcutaneous fat loss, muscular prominence, acanthosis nigricans, and hepatic steatosis. Metreleptin is not drawn. Low leptin is the reason replacement is used in generalized lipodystrophy. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: New diabetes in an older thin adult can be the first sign of **pancreatic cancer**. Steroid hyperglycemia and post-transplant diabetes are secondary. **Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes** is treated with **insulin**, and screening is an annual OGTT from about age 10, not HbA1c alone. Weight loss with new diabetes is a reason to think of the pancreas.
